- When sentiment is consistently high (>0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by rapid decline, it often overcorrects; cap forecast peak at 1–2% above recent high.
- In low sentiment (below 0.4) or negative sentiment, model frequently underestimates; add 3–5% to forecast to account for downward bias.
- Model tends to lag in early periods (first 3–5 days of forecast) — adjust downward by 1–2% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is volatile or erratic, model overfits short-term noise; smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 values before final output.
- When true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., after 70–75% of forecast range), reduce forecast by 2–5% to avoid over-optimistic extrapolation.
- If sentiment history shows rising optimism (e.g., 0.6–0.8 over 3+ days), model often overshoots; apply downward correction of 3–7% on peak days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from 15-day moving average, adjust forecast to align with recent trend, not just historical mean.
